raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
## Purpose

Related to #58636. This patch replaces the separately compiled GLM5Next indexer key-normalization leaf with the existing `LayerNorm` module. It preserves fp32 normalization, the same weight/bias/epsilon, and the activation-dtype cast-back, without changing checkpoint names or private/global Inductor configuration. Pointwise compiled leaves remain unchanged.

The goal is to remove rank-local reduction autotuning from a replicated key path, where differing reduction orders can change near-tie sparse selections. This is a conservative correctness candidate. Reporter-provided eager-mode rank-agreement results are now available for the production file at the current head, as detailed below. Full-head CUDA tests, model accuracy, and serving benchmarks remain outstanding.

### Why this is not duplicate work

The issue is unassigned and its complete discussion contains no implementation claim. Fresh searches for #58636 and the norm leaf found no matching PR. Nearby row-sharding work (#54394, #54951, #58536) does not change this leaf and retains replicated fallback paths. #57815 concerns downstream batch-invariant top-k behavior; #54851 changes captured KV-cache writes in `deepseek_v32/attention.py`, not this GLM5Next norm.

## Test Plan

```sh
VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu PYTHONPATH="$PWD" PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
  .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/models/glm5next/test_sparse_indexer_topk_dispatch.py \
  tests/test_config.py \
  -k 'kpool or test_breakable_cudagraph_platform_default' -q -rs
.venv/bin/python -m pre_commit run --files \
  vllm/models/glm5next/common/attention.py \
  tests/models/glm5next/test_sparse_indexer_topk_dispatch.py \
  tests/test_config.py
git diff --check
```

## Test Result

On Apple Silicon with CPU PyTorch 2.13.0, rerun on October 11, 2026 at `fcbbd5b7`: **21 passed, 18 skipped, 421 deselected**. The 18 skips are four CUDA dispatch, eight ROCm dispatch, and six CUDA/graph validation cases. This assistant-run CPU check does not satisfy the submitting-human or GPU requirements. Applicable pre-commit hooks and whitespace checks passed during the prior branch update.

The new regression reaches normalization through a real tiny `Indexer.forward`, real projection layers and single-rank Gloo. A hook stops immediately after normalization, before unavailable GPU-only quantization/indexer operations. It checks strided keys, fp32/fp16/bf16 inputs and nontrivial fp32 parameters against explicit fp32 `F.layer_norm`.

Before the change, the CPU regression fails at the compiled norm under `torch.compiler.set_stance("fail_on_recompile")`; after the change, all six CPU normalization cases pass. This proves removal of that compilation path and the CPU numeric contract, **not** reproduction or resolution of the reported GPU numerical divergence. Four existing CUDA dispatch cases and six new CUDA/graph-replay cases are skipped locally.

## External validation update (October 11, 2026)

[The reporter's October 5 report](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58979#issuecomment-5998912306) includes [raw logs and exact configuration](https://gist.github.com/Bizuayeu/0caa413f62be892150d83d4376990a3e). The baseline was `138810056093301f4881050fcf2b1786939da387`; the candidate used the same image with `attention.py` from `fcbbd5b7b5f56f50910216d76f9e45f3c019fba0`. This was reporter-run testing of the production change, not a local run of the full PR test suite.

Across eight fresh baseline launches, replicated keys differed in four launches and candidate sets differed in one. Across four candidate launches, keys and candidate sets agreed at every traced call. Both arms had within-launch greedy-completion variation from other paths, so those completion hashes do not demonstrate model-output equivalence. Reported token rates were explicitly not a serving benchmark.

The requested `lm_eval` accuracy evaluation and `vllm bench serve` comparison with raw output logs remain pending, as do the new CUDA/graph-replay tests. The available local machine is an Apple M4 with CPU PyTorch (`torch.cuda.is_available() == False`, zero CUDA devices), not suitable hardware for these runs. No GPU or model result is inferred from CPU checks. The separate October 6 older-pin/alternative-implementation report is not validation of this PR head.

## Required follow-up before ready for review / merge

- [ ] Run the CUDA norm and graph-replay cases.
- [x] Reporter supplied matched two-GB10 TP2 fresh-launch rank traces and completion hashes for main plus the current production file. The completion hashes did not isolate this change's effect; see limitations below.
- [ ] Run GLM model evaluation and prefill/decode performance measurements. Native normalization can add launches/memory traffic relative to the fused leaf; no performance non-regression is claimed.
- [ ] Complete submitting-human test/model validation under the contribution policy.

Default non-ROCm GLM5Next architectures use breakable CUDA graphs with `CompilationMode.NONE`; the config regression covers these defaults. Explicit opt-out/full-model compilation configurations are not claimed as validated.

## AI assistance

Prepared and independently code-reviewed with OpenAI Codex. The submitter confirmed reviewing the code and explicitly requested this draft. The local CPU tests and lint above were run by the assistant; the submitter has not personally rerun the tests. Human test/model validation and GPU verification remain outstanding and are not asserted complete.

---

<summary>Essential Elements of an Effective PR Description Checklist</summary>

- [x] Purpose and issue link included.
- [x] Test commands included.
- [x] Available results and validation limits included.
- [ ] Required hardware/model validation completed.
</details>

Thanks — I ran it on the two-GB10 pair.

**Setup.** I applied only the `attention.py` hunk of 678a805795 to our pinned image (vLLM `385dce36`, where the file is `glm5next/nvidia/attention.py`, plus our local patches unrelated to this path), not the PR's head. Same model, profile and image as our serving setup (TP=2, MTP depth 3, `--enforce-eager`, temperature 0), except that I turned our Inductor deterministic workaround off, so the remaining compiled leaves pick their configs by timing on each rank, as they did when we saw the three states. Three fresh launches, all eager, and then one launch with decode CUDA graphs.

**Rank agreement.** In each launch, a traced request compares the key and the candidate set that the indexer op receives on the two ranks at every call:

| Launch | Calls where the ranks' keys differ | Calls where the candidate sets differ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 of 858 | 0 |
| 2 | 0 of 858 | 0 |
| 3 | 0 of 858 | 0 |

No key-norm kernel is among the Inductor kernels the workers serve. The only compiled kernel whose config differed between the ranks is one that already differed while we were in state 1.

**Completions.** Our fixed greedy prompts (three prompts, three repeats each) gave identical completions within each launch and across the three launches. One of the three differs from what our serving setup gives with the fused leaf pinned to `XBLOCK=8`. The eager norm sums the rows in a different order, and the fused and eager outputs differ in bits at 2,048 rows. I read that difference as expected; the ranks agree with each other.

**Performance.** Decode throughput was within −2.0 % to +0.6 % of our setup with the workaround, measured five hours earlier the same day. A run of our setup right after them landed in the same band (−2.1 % to −0.7 %), so I can't attribute a difference to the change. The 65,536-token prefill in our warmup took 53.7–54.7 s, against 53.5 s before and 53.9 s after. In isolation on one GB10, same image, strided `(rows, 160)[:, :128]` bf16 input:

| Rows | Wall time per call, no CUDA graph: fused / this PR | GPU time per call in a CUDA graph: fused / this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1–8 | 19–20 µs / 13.3–13.6 µs | 1.4–1.6 µs / 4.3–5.7 µs |
| 2,048 | 20 µs / 20.5 µs | 4.5 µs / 14.1 µs |

Without CUDA graphs, the compiled wrapper costs more per call than the two extra kernels do, so this PR is faster there. With CUDA graphs it adds a few µs per call, which I estimate at around 0.1 % of a decode step.

**CUDA graphs.** One more launch with the same change and the workaround off, with decode captured as a full CUDA graph (`cudagraph_mode` `FULL_DECODE_ONLY`, compilation mode NONE, one sequence). It gave the same completions as the three eager launches. Hooks don't run inside a replayed graph, so the trace compares only the prefill calls: the keys and candidate sets agreed on all 22. Decode was 2.6–4.1 % slower than the eager launches, the direction we saw before for graphs on this model and hardware, so I can't separate this PR's few µs from that.

Not run:

- **The CUDA test cases added in the PR.** Our pair runs a pinned image (vLLM `385dce36`), where this module is `glm5next/nvidia/attention.py` and the tests' imports don't resolve. Running them would need a build of the PR head for GB10 (aarch64, sm_121), which I haven't done.
- **Rank agreement at decode under CUDA graphs**, beyond the completions: the trace can't see inside a replayed graph. Our graph option captures decode for one sequence only, and we serve eager because graphs were slower per step here.
- **A full-model compile.** We don't use it, and the PR doesn't claim it. Under such a configuration Inductor would compile this norm again, so its reduction config would again be chosen on each rank, unless Inductor's deterministic mode is on — which pytorch/pytorch#198563 currently turns off after the first compiled frame.

@yewentao256, could you review this draft's normalization approach when convenient? The reporter tested the production hunk on a pinned two-GB10 image, while testing the full PR head is still outstanding. Thank you!

**Command.** Both arms used the same command (`serve-command-rank0.txt` in the gist; rank 1 adds `--headless` and its own address):

```
vllm serve <model> --distributed-executor-backend mp --nnodes 2 --tensor-parallel-size 2 --node-rank 0 \

```

Inductor's deterministic mode is off (its default). Each launch is a new container with an empty `~/.cache`, so Inductor and Triton compile and autotune from scratch every time.

Two things differ from a completely plain launch:
- **The model directory.** It is `nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4` at `423acf37`, with `"*.layers.45.*"` added to the quantization exclude list in `config.json` and `hf_quant_config.json`; all the other files are links to the snapshot. Without that line, main fails to load the BF16 MTP layer, and both errors are in the gist:
  - with the draft on triton: `moe_backend='triton' is not supported for NvFP4 MoE`
  - with marlin: a 512/1024 shape mismatch in `glm5next/common/mtp.py`

- **The probe.** `rank_probe.py` (in the gist) is a worker extension loaded with `--worker-extension-cls` and reached through `/collective_rpc` (`VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1`). On main, the ranks handed the indexer op different keys in 4 of the 8 launches (11 to 16 calls each). In one of them (mc7) this also changed the candidate set on 7 calls. In each of those four launches, one rank picked `XBLOCK 1` for the key-norm kernel and the other picked `XBLOCK 8`. The launches that picked 8/32, 8/8, 32/8 or 32/32 agreed on every call.

On the PR, no key-norm kernel is autotuned on either rank. The only kernel left is a pointwise one (`z4/d96443a1`), whose pick also differs between ranks at times. All four launches agreed on every call.

**Completion hashes.** The per-launch hashes are in `decode9-*.jsonl` in the gist: three prompts, three greedy samples each, 512 tokens. They don't discriminate here. On main and on the PR alike, the three samples of every prompt gave three different completions within a single launch. So something other than this norm makes plain main give different completions across requests here, and the completion hashes can't show this PR's effect; our pinned build pins those paths locally. The rank trace is the evidence for this PR.

Decode speed, as the median of the per-launch medians in tok/s (prose / counting / code), not a benchmark:
- main: 22.35 / 33.15 / 30.23
- PR: 22.50 / 32.77 / 29.78

**Launches not counted.**
- A smoke launch of main, with the same pattern: 8/1 gave 14 differing calls.
- One attempt with a 2 GiB KV cache and the 262,144 window (`mb1` in the log), which refused to start because one request at that length needs 2.48 GiB of KV cache; hence the 131,072 window.
- A first chain with a 3 GiB KV cache and a 262,144 window, stopped after its first PR launch. Our host memory guard killed that launch at 4 GiB free, because rank 0 sat at 5–6 GiB free there. In that chain, 8/32 gave 0 differing calls and 8/1 gave 14, plus 3 differing candidate sets.

The chain's 12 launches all used the 2 GiB / 131,072 command shown above.

Items 2 and 3 remain as I said: `lm_eval` and `vllm bench serve` at TP=2 on GB10 with one sequence would say little about performance, so they are better run on the usual hardware.

Some data from a second 2× GB10 pair (TP=2 over RoCE, `RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4`, vLLM `4be061c5` built from source, torch 2.13.0+cu130). It is at an older pin than the PR head, so it is context for the review, not validation of `fcbbd5b7`.

**A standalone test can miss this.** We first tried the mechanism outside the model: vLLM's compiled `_fused_indexer_k_norm` on a fixed 2048×160 bf16 input sliced to 128 columns, 40 fresh processes with Inductor caches disabled. All 40 gave identical output, because in that setting Inductor generated a looped reduction, not the persistent reduction with XBLOCK 1/8/32 candidates that it generates inside the served model. A unit test for this fix should check which kernel is generated, or run in-model.

**Final answers, not only rank traces.** @Bizuayeu noted that completion hashes can't discriminate on plain main, because answers vary between requests within a launch. Our build pins the two other sources of that variation locally: the MoE fused finalize (cf. #54948) and the indexer top-k tie order (cf. #54521 / #55122). With those in place, long prompts (3,633 and 9,819 tokens) gave the same answer every time within a session, but 9 of 32 server sessions gave one of three other answers. Short prompts never varied. In an odd session the only rank difference on the indexer path was the normed key, in 1–7 of 2,048 rows per indexer layer; the indexer input, the `wk` projection and the gate scores were identical on both ranks. The odd sessions had XBLOCK 1 picked on one rank or on both.

**An alternative that keeps the fused kernel.** Passing `options={"deterministic": True}` in `_INDEXER_COMPILE` is applied during that leaf's code generation, so the Dynamo reset from pytorch#198563 does not undo it. Inductor then picks one reduction config by rule on every rank, with no benchmarking. We ran 12 starts: 7 with the patched file mounted and 5 cold starts of a rebuilt image. In all 12, neither rank saved a k-norm `.best_config`, every generated kernel was `deterministic: True`, and there was one answer, the same as in the usual sessions. So users already on the common answer see no change. Decode speed was 15.44 vs 15.48 tok/s (median of 5, switch on vs off). Compared with this PR, ours keeps the bits identical to the common case, while the PR does not depend on Inductor's config-selection rules. Either looks fine to us. We are happy to share the patch. If it would help and our two nodes are free at the time, we could also run the PR's `attention.py` through the same boot loop at our pin.

Raw per-boot logs available on request.

detail.body:
## Purpose

Related to #58636. This patch replaces the separately compiled GLM5Next indexer key-normalization leaf with the existing `LayerNorm` module. It preserves fp32 normalization, the same weight/bias/epsilon, and the activation-dtype cast-back, without changing checkpoint names or private/global Inductor configuration. Pointwise compiled leaves remain unchanged.

The goal is to remove rank-local reduction autotuning from a replicated key path, where differing reduction orders can change near-tie sparse selections. This is a conservative correctness candidate. Reporter-provided eager-mode rank-agreement results are now available for the production file at the current head, as detailed below. Full-head CUDA tests, model accuracy, and serving benchmarks remain outstanding.

### Why this is not duplicate work

The issue is unassigned and its complete discussion contains no implementation claim. Fresh searches for #58636 and the norm leaf found no matching PR. Nearby row-sharding work (#54394, #54951, #58536) does not change this leaf and retains replicated fallback paths. #57815 concerns downstream batch-invariant top-k behavior; #54851 changes captured KV-cache writes in `deepseek_v32/attention.py`, not this GLM5Next norm.

## Test Plan

```sh
VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE=cpu PYTHONPATH="$PWD" PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
  .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/models/glm5next/test_sparse_indexer_topk_dispatch.py \
  tests/test_config.py \
  -k 'kpool or test_breakable_cudagraph_platform_default' -q -rs
.venv/bin/python -m pre_commit run --files \
  vllm/models/glm5next/common/attention.py \
  tests/models/glm5next/test_sparse_indexer_topk_dispatch.py \
  tests/test_config.py
git diff --check
```

## Test Result

On Apple Silicon with CPU PyTorch 2.13.0, rerun on October 11, 2026 at `fcbbd5b7`: **21 passed, 18 skipped, 421 deselected**. The 18 skips are four CUDA dispatch, eight ROCm dispatch, and six CUDA/graph validation cases. This assistant-run CPU check does not satisfy the submitting-human or GPU requirements. Applicable pre-commit hooks and whitespace checks passed during the prior branch update.

The new regression reaches normalization through a real tiny `Indexer.forward`, real projection layers and single-rank Gloo. A hook stops immediately after normalization, before unavailable GPU-only quantization/indexer operations. It checks strided keys, fp32/fp16/bf16 inputs and nontrivial fp32 parameters against explicit fp32 `F.layer_norm`.

Before the change, the CPU regression fails at the compiled norm under `torch.compiler.set_stance("fail_on_recompile")`; after the change, all six CPU normalization cases pass. This proves removal of that compilation path and the CPU numeric contract, **not** reproduction or resolution of the reported GPU numerical divergence. Four existing CUDA dispatch cases and six new CUDA/graph-replay cases are skipped locally.

## External validation update (October 11, 2026)

[The reporter's October 5 report](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58979#issuecomment-5998912306) includes [raw logs and exact configuration](https://gist.github.com/Bizuayeu/0caa413f62be892150d83d4376990a3e). The baseline was `138810056093301f4881050fcf2b1786939da387`; the candidate used the same image with `attention.py` from `fcbbd5b7b5f56f50910216d76f9e45f3c019fba0`. This was reporter-run testing of the production change, not a local run of the full PR test suite.

Across eight fresh baseline launches, replicated keys differed in four launches and candidate sets differed in one. Across four candidate launches, keys and candidate sets agreed at every traced call. Both arms had within-launch greedy-completion variation from other paths, so those completion hashes do not demonstrate model-output equivalence. Reported token rates were explicitly not a serving benchmark.

The requested `lm_eval` accuracy evaluation and `vllm bench serve` comparison with raw output logs remain pending, as do the new CUDA/graph-replay tests. The available local machine is an Apple M4 with CPU PyTorch (`torch.cuda.is_available() == False`, zero CUDA devices), not suitable hardware for these runs. No GPU or model result is inferred from CPU checks. The separate October 6 older-pin/alternative-implementation report is not validation of this PR head.

## Required follow-up before ready for review / merge

- [ ] Run the CUDA norm and graph-replay cases.
- [x] Reporter supplied matched two-GB10 TP2 fresh-launch rank traces and completion hashes for main plus the current production file. The completion hashes did not isolate this change's effect; see limitations below.
- [ ] Run GLM model evaluation and prefill/decode performance measurements. Native normalization can add launches/memory traffic relative to the fused leaf; no performance non-regression is claimed.
- [ ] Complete submitting-human test/model validation under the contribution policy.

Default non-ROCm GLM5Next architectures use breakable CUDA graphs with `CompilationMode.NONE`; the config regression covers these defaults. Explicit opt-out/full-model compilation configurations are not claimed as validated.

## AI assistance

Prepared and independently code-reviewed with OpenAI Codex. The submitter confirmed reviewing the code and explicitly requested this draft. The local CPU tests and lint above were run by the assistant; the submitter has not personally rerun the tests. Human test/model validation and GPU verification remain outstanding and are not asserted complete.

- [x] Available results and validation limits included.
- [ ] Required hardware/model validation completed.
</details>

+            cache_config=CacheConfig(block_size=512),
+            topk_indices_buffer=torch.empty(num_tokens, 512, dtype=torch.int32),

+        )
+        hidden = torch.randn(num_tokens, 8)
+    for layer in (indexer.wq_b, indexer.wk_weights_proj):
+        layer.weight.normal_()
+    indexer._wp_fp32 = (
+        indexer.wk_weights_proj.weight[indexer.head_dim :, :].t().contiguous().float()
+    )
+    for layer in (indexer.wq_b, indexer.wk_weights_proj):
+        layer.quant_method.process_weights_after_loading(layer)
+    indexer.k_norm.weight.normal_()
+    indexer.k_norm.bias.normal_()
+
+    captured = []
+
+    class NormReached(Exception):
+        pass
+
+    def stop_after_norm(module, args, output):
+        captured.append((args[0], output))
+        raise NormReached
+
+    torch.compiler.reset()
+    with (
+        indexer.k_norm.register_forward_hook(stop_after_norm),
+        pytest.raises(NormReached),
+        torch.compiler.set_stance("fail_on_recompile"),
+    ):
+        indexer(hidden, hidden, positions=None, rotary_emb=None)
+
+    key, output = captured[0]
+    assert key.stride() == (160, 1)
+    assert output.dtype == dtype
+    assert indexer.k_norm.weight.dtype == indexer.k_norm.bias.dtype == torch.float32
+    expected = torch.nn.functional.layer_norm(
+        key.float(), (128,), indexer.k_norm.weight, indexer.k_norm.bias, 1e-6
+    ).to(dtype)
+    torch.testing.assert_close(output, expected, rtol=0, atol=0)
+
+    if device == "cuda":
+        with torch.cuda.stream(torch.cuda.Stream()):

issue_comments.body:
Thanks — I ran it on the two-GB10 pair.

**Setup.** I applied only the `attention.py` hunk of 678a805795 to our pinned image (vLLM `385dce36`, where the file is `glm5next/nvidia/attention.py`, plus our local patches unrelated to this path), not the PR's head. Same model, profile and image as our serving setup (TP=2, MTP depth 3, `--enforce-eager`, temperature 0), except that I turned our Inductor deterministic workaround off, so the remaining compiled leaves pick their configs by timing on each rank, as they did when we saw the three states. Three fresh launches, all eager, and then one launch with decode CUDA graphs.

**Rank agreement.** In each launch, a traced request compares the key and the candidate set that the indexer op receives on the two ranks at every call:

| Launch | Calls where the ranks' keys differ | Calls where the candidate sets differ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 of 858 | 0 |
| 2 | 0 of 858 | 0 |
| 3 | 0 of 858 | 0 |

No key-norm kernel is among the Inductor kernels the workers serve. The only compiled kernel whose config differed between the ranks is one that already differed while we were in state 1.

**Completions.** Our fixed greedy prompts (three prompts, three repeats each) gave identical completions within each launch and across the three launches. One of the three differs from what our serving setup gives with the fused leaf pinned to `XBLOCK=8`. The eager norm sums the rows in a different order, and the fused and eager outputs differ in bits at 2,048 rows. I read that difference as expected; the ranks agree with each other.

**Performance.** Decode throughput was within −2.0 % to +0.6 % of our setup with the workaround, measured five hours earlier the same day. A run of our setup right after them landed in the same band (−2.1 % to −0.7 %), so I can't attribute a difference to the change. The 65,536-token prefill in our warmup took 53.7–54.7 s, against 53.5 s before and 53.9 s after. In isolation on one GB10, same image, strided `(rows, 160)[:, :128]` bf16 input:

| Rows | Wall time per call, no CUDA graph: fused / this PR | GPU time per call in a CUDA graph: fused / this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1–8 | 19–20 µs / 13.3–13.6 µs | 1.4–1.6 µs / 4.3–5.7 µs |
| 2,048 | 20 µs / 20.5 µs | 4.5 µs / 14.1 µs |

Without CUDA graphs, the compiled wrapper costs more per call than the two extra kernels do, so this PR is faster there. With CUDA graphs it adds a few µs per call, which I estimate at around 0.1 % of a decode step.

**CUDA graphs.** One more launch with the same change and the workaround off, with decode captured as a full CUDA graph (`cudagraph_mode` `FULL_DECODE_ONLY`, compilation mode NONE, one sequence). It gave the same completions as the three eager launches. Hooks don't run inside a replayed graph, so the trace compares only the prefill calls: the keys and candidate sets agreed on all 22. Decode was 2.6–4.1 % slower than the eager launches, the direction we saw before for graphs on this model and hardware, so I can't separate this PR's few µs from that.

Not run:

- **The CUDA test cases added in the PR.** Our pair runs a pinned image (vLLM `385dce36`), where this module is `glm5next/nvidia/attention.py` and the tests' imports don't resolve. Running them would need a build of the PR head for GB10 (aarch64, sm_121), which I haven't done.
- **Rank agreement at decode under CUDA graphs**, beyond the completions: the trace can't see inside a replayed graph. Our graph option captures decode for one sequence only, and we serve eager because graphs were slower per step here.
- **A full-model compile.** We don't use it, and the PR doesn't claim it. Under such a configuration Inductor would compile this norm again, so its reduction config would again be chosen on each rank, unless Inductor's deterministic mode is on — which pytorch/pytorch#198563 currently turns off after the first compiled frame.

@yewentao256, could you review this draft's normalization approach when convenient? The reporter tested the production hunk on a pinned two-GB10 image, while testing the full PR head is still outstanding. Thank you!

- **The model directory.** It is `nvidia/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4` at `423acf37`, with `"*.layers.45.*"` added to the quantization exclude list in `config.json` and `hf_quant_config.json`; all the other files are links to the snapshot. Without that line, main fails to load the BF16 MTP layer, and both errors are in the gist:
  - with the draft on triton: `moe_backend='triton' is not supported for NvFP4 MoE`
  - with marlin: a 512/1024 shape mismatch in `glm5next/common/mtp.py`

  The checkpoint's later revision `da920bb0b9` declares that layer itself; we did not use it.
- **The probe.** `rank_probe.py` (in the gist) is a worker extension loaded with `--worker-extension-cls` and reached through `/collective_rpc` (`VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE=1`). It only reads tensors, in forward hooks. For one request (a 2,108-token prompt and 160 greedy tokens), each rank fingerprints, at every call of every layer's indexer op, the key the op receives and the candidate set it returns. `rank_keys.py` then compares the two ranks call by call.

**Rank agreement.** Below, condensed from the raw files (`<label>-rank_keys.txt`, `<label>-picks-r0.txt`, `<label>-picks-r1.txt` in the gist; `INDEX.txt` lists them), is each launch's `rank_keys.py` line, followed by the autotuned config each rank picked for the key-norm kernel: the Inductor kernel whose generated source contains `layer_norm`, read from its `.best_config`.

On main, the ranks handed the indexer op different keys in 4 of the 8 launches (11 to 16 calls each). In one of them (mc7) this also changed the candidate set on 7 calls. In each of those four launches, one rank picked `XBLOCK 1` for the key-norm kernel and the other picked `XBLOCK 8`. The launches that picked 8/32, 8/8, 32/8 or 32/32 agreed on every call.

On the PR, no key-norm kernel is autotuned on either rank. The only kernel left is a pointwise one (`z4/d96443a1`), whose pick also differs between ranks at times. All four launches agreed on every call.

**Completion hashes.** The per-launch hashes are in `decode9-*.jsonl` in the gist: three prompts, three greedy samples each, 512 tokens. They don't discriminate here. On main and on the PR alike, the three samples of every prompt gave three different completions within a single launch. So something other than this norm makes plain main give different completions across requests here, and the completion hashes can't show this PR's effect; our pinned build pins those paths locally. The rank trace is the evidence for this PR.

Decode speed, as the median of the per-launch medians in tok/s (prose / counting / code), not a benchmark:
- main: 22.35 / 33.15 / 30.23
- PR: 22.50 / 32.77 / 29.78

**Launches not counted.**
- A smoke launch of main, with the same pattern: 8/1 gave 14 differing calls.
- One attempt with a 2 GiB KV cache and the 262,144 window (`mb1` in the log), which refused to start because one request at that length needs 2.48 GiB of KV cache; hence the 131,072 window.
- A first chain with a 3 GiB KV cache and a 262,144 window, stopped after its first PR launch. Our host memory guard killed that launch at 4 GiB free, because rank 0 sat at 5–6 GiB free there. In that chain, 8/32 gave 0 differing calls and 8/1 gave 14, plus 3 differing candidate sets.

The chain's 12 launches all used the 2 GiB / 131,072 command shown above.

Items 2 and 3 remain as I said: `lm_eval` and `vllm bench serve` at TP=2 on GB10 with one sequence would say little about performance, so they are better run on the usual hardware.

Some data from a second 2× GB10 pair (TP=2 over RoCE, `RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4`, vLLM `4be061c5` built from source, torch 2.13.0+cu130). It is at an older pin than the PR head, so it is context for the review, not validation of `fcbbd5b7`.

**A standalone test can miss this.** We first tried the mechanism outside the model: vLLM's compiled `_fused_indexer_k_norm` on a fixed 2048×160 bf16 input sliced to 128 columns, 40 fresh processes with Inductor caches disabled. All 40 gave identical output, because in that setting Inductor generated a looped reduction, not the persistent reduction with XBLOCK 1/8/32 candidates that it generates inside the served model. A unit test for this fix should check which kernel is generated, or run in-model.

**Final answers, not only rank traces.** @Bizuayeu noted that completion hashes can't discriminate on plain main, because answers vary between requests within a launch. Our build pins the two other sources of that variation locally: the MoE fused finalize (cf. #54948) and the indexer top-k tie order (cf. #54521 / #55122). With those in place, long prompts (3,633 and 9,819 tokens) gave the same answer every time within a session, but 9 of 32 server sessions gave one of three other answers. Short prompts never varied. In an odd session the only rank difference on the indexer path was the normed key, in 1–7 of 2,048 rows per indexer layer; the indexer input, the `wk` projection and the gate scores were identical on both ranks. The odd sessions had XBLOCK 1 picked on one rank or on both.

**An alternative that keeps the fused kernel.** Passing `options={"deterministic": True}` in `_INDEXER_COMPILE` is applied during that leaf's code generation, so the Dynamo reset from pytorch#198563 does not undo it. Inductor then picks one reduction config by rule on every rank, with no benchmarking. We ran 12 starts: 7 with the patched file mounted and 5 cold starts of a rebuilt image. In all 12, neither rank saved a k-norm `.best_config`, every generated kernel was `deterministic: True`, and there was one answer, the same as in the usual sessions. So users already on the common answer see no change. Decode speed was 15.44 vs 15.48 tok/s (median of 5, switch on vs off). Compared with this PR, ours keeps the bits identical to the common case, while the PR does not depend on Inductor's config-selection rules. Either looks fine to us. We are happy to share the patch. If it would help and our two nodes are free at the time, we could also run the PR's `attention.py` through the same boot loop at our pin.

Raw per-boot logs available on request.
